A code comment directly above line 1483 explains the `always()` addition: because these jobs have `needs: probe`/`needs: implement-probe`, a bare `needs:` would silently SKIP the dependent job if concurrency cancellation cancelled the upstream tier job; `always()` keeps the job running so an empty consumed allowlist routes to the helper's 'unestablished' arm rather than a silent skip. Ran python3 scripts/subagent-write-probe-verdict.py against constructed execution-file fixtures in a temp dir to attempt falsification of the docstring's exhaustiveness claim (lines 105-140 and 96-101 of scripts/subagent-write-probe-verdict.py). (a) A Write denial with tool_name='Write' naming neither the side-effect filename nor the payload routed to `_is_unclassified_write_denied` -> compute() line 703-714 emitted verdict='unestablished' with the exact named reason 'its text names neither subwrite-review.txt nor the probe's payload marker'. (b) A denial entry with NO tool_name naming an unrelated path (no filename, no payload) fell through all four per-entry classifiers (_is_dispatch_denial/_is_write_denial/_is_foreign_write_denial/_is_unclassified_write_denial all False) and was silently dropped from every bucket -- but this is explicitly disclosed in the docstring's own line 101 ('otherwise neither') and correctly has ZERO effect on the verdict (the run instead resolved via the co-recorded tool_use Write, unaffected by the useless denial); it is not an unnamed reachable verdict state, since it never drives verdict selection at all. (c) A parent-less Write naming the side-effect file, co-recorded with a Task dispatch that no call chains to, produced verdict='unestablished' via the chain_attributable=False arm (compute() line 674-685), with a named reason citing the 'distinct third schema world'. (d) Constructed a genuine DENIED case (Write denial naming the filename, tool_name='Write', dispatch recorded, no parent-less orchestrator Write) and confirmed DENIED is only reached via the guarded elif at line 614-639, which requires write_denied AND dispatch_recorded AND not orchestrator_write_recorded (the two preceding guard arms at line 592 and 604 intercept the unguarded cases into unestablished first). Code inspection of compute() (lines 372-745) shows the verdict is derived by a single if/elif/.../else chain over boolean conditions, which is exhaustive by construction in Python -- every input necessarily reaches exactly one arm, and every arm assigns both a verdict string and a specific reason string (confirmed by reading all 19 arms). The trailing fail-closed check (line 737-745, outside _VERDICTS) and main()'s catch-all exception handler (line 977-988) additionally cover the two residual non-arm failure classes (a typo'd/invalid verdict string, and an unexpected exception), both named in the docstring's enumeration and both producing their own reason text. No reachable code path was found that produces a verdict with no reason, and no path was found that produces DENIED outside the (write_denied, dispatch_recorded, no-orchestrator-write) triple.

The comment at .github/workflows/matcher-probe.yml:1444-1459 says a Write record has 'exactly one EXPECTED author (the subagent)' and immediately qualifies this: 'That is a PROMPT-level guarantee, not a technical restriction — the composed allowlist grants Write(.devflow/tmp/**) to the whole session, so the orchestrator keeps the capability and is simply not asked to use it. The verdict helper does not rest on the prompt alone: wherever the execution file records parent chains, a parent-less (orchestrator-issued) Write naming the same file falsifies the premise and routes the run to unestablished instead of a DENIED that record would contradict.' I built two falsification fixtures against scripts/subagent-write-probe-verdict.py to test this: (1) an execution file with a dispatch, a chain-attributable subagent call (so chains_are_recorded=True), a parent-less orchestrator-issued Write naming the side-effect file, and a Write permission_denials entry naming the same file — the helper correctly emitted `unestablished` ('a parent-less (orchestrator-issued) Write naming the same file was recorded too — the no-orchestrator-write premise ... is falsified'), NOT DENIED, matching subagent-write-probe-verdict.py:604-613. (2) an execution file with no parent_tool_use_id recorded anywhere (chains_are_recorded=False) plus a dispatch and a Write denial naming the side-effect file — the helper emitted DENIED (subagent-write-probe-verdict.py:614-639), with its own reason text explicitly stating 'this file records no parent_tool_use_id at all, so whether an orchestrator-issued Write names that file is unestablished rather than ruled out' — i.e. DENIED is emitted here precisely because orchestrator_write_recorded is False for reasons of ignorance (code comment lines 621-625: 'a parent-less Write cannot be told from a subagent's ... asserting "no orchestrator-issued Write names that file" would publish an unknown as a measured zero'). The workflow comment's universal survives because it is explicitly hedged with the word EXPECTED and is immediately followed, in the same comment block, by an admission that this is a prompt-level (not technical) guarantee, that the orchestrator retains the Write capability, and that the verdict helper only catches the falsifying case 'wherever the execution file records parent chains' — leaving the no-chains residual (case 2) undisclosed as an explicit gap but not contradicted, since the comment never claims the check works in the absence of recorded chains. I confirmed (via the comment's own text, cross-checked against the review/implement tiers' needs: consumed allowlist composition described at lines 1461-1468) that the composed allowlist does grant Write to the whole session, exactly as the comment states, which is the basis for calling this an EXPECTED (not enforced) single-author premise.

matcher-probe.yml's two verdict steps (lines 1579-1605 and 1687-1713) both run 'set -euo pipefail' then 'EXTRA=()', conditionally append '--upstream-tools-empty', and unconditionally expand "${EXTRA[@]}" with no ${arr[@]+...} guard. All jobs in this file declare 'runs-on: ubuntu-latest' (confirmed via grep at lines 105,494,969,1059,1152,1217,1264,1358,1486,1613), and GitHub-hosted ubuntu-latest runners ship bash 5.1+ (22.04) or 5.2+ (24.04), both well past the bash 4.4 fix where an empty array expanded via "${arr[@]}" under set -u no longer aborts as unbound. The repo itself documents the underlying hazard and the guarded fallback pattern in scripts/validate-telemetry-artifact.sh:146-147 ('bash 3.2 aborts on "${arr[@]}" when empty under set -u ... every expansion uses the ${arr[@]+"${arr[@]}"} guarded form'), but that script must remain portable to macOS's default bash 3.2, a concern that does not apply to matcher-probe.yml which only ever executes on ubuntu-latest's modern bash. So the unguarded pattern is safe in this specific context, matching the claim.

The first half of the claim accurately describes collect()'s assumption: scripts/subagent-write-probe-verdict.py:301-336 threads parent_tool_use_id down from an enclosing dict as `inherited` (an envelope value) into nested tool_use blocks, and the code comment (lines 303-313) states verbatim '`parent_tool_use_id` is recorded on the MESSAGE ENVELOPE, not on the `tool_use` block ... the block itself carries only type/id/name/input.' Denial entries are read via `d.get("tool_name")` (line 357) consistent with the tool_name/tool_input claim. However, the claim's closing sentence -- 'These are the shapes a real claude-code-action execution file uses' -- asserts this envelope-nesting shape is CONFIRMED by the cited committed census, and it is not: the same code comment explicitly says 'The committed census cannot settle this: docs/execution-file-shape.md records that its flattened, uniqued key set "erases parentage"' (lines 312-313). docs/execution-file-shape.md itself states the observed structural key set is flattened/uniqued and 'erases parentage' (its only use of that phrase, in the per-message-usage row, generalizes to every key), and its per-field evidence for `tool_use` events (docs/execution-file-shape.md line 58) lists a DIFFERENT key vocabulary -- `tool_name`, `tool_input`, `tool_use_id`, `tool_uses` -- not the `type`/`id`/`name`/`input` shape the code assumes for the nested block; docs/execution-file-shape.observed.txt's flattened key list contains BOTH vocabularies (type/id/name/input at lines 60,62,77,138 AND tool_name/tool_input/tool_use_id at lines 126-128) with no way to tell which object each set attaches to. lib/test/run.sh independently corroborates that this is an unproven pinned assumption, not an observed fact: its 'PRODUCTION NESTING' fixture comment (~line 24587) states 'The committed census cannot settle this ... so these fixtures pin the resolution on the shape the helper will actually meet' -- i.e. the shape is asserted/pinned, not verified against the committed evidence. So checked against the exact verify_against sources, the claim's assertion that these are confirmed real shapes is false; the code's own documentation (and the test suite) is honest that this is an unverified assumption.

The claim asserts the #858 fixtures (flat + envelope-nested) 'match the real execution-file shape the helper will meet in production', but neither of the two sources the item names as verify_against actually establishes that for the envelope-nested shape. (1) docs/execution-file-shape.observed.txt / docs/execution-file-shape.md: the census is explicitly flattened+uniqued and, per the doc's own text ('the flattened, unique'd key set erases parentage, so the per-message attachment of these keys is a schema-level observation ... not something the committed artifact itself can prove'), cannot confirm or deny WHERE parent_tool_use_id sits (envelope vs. tool_use block) or that message.content[] nesting is real. lib/test/run.sh's own comment at the envelope_permitted fixture (line ~24592) says the same thing verbatim: 'The committed census cannot settle this ... so these fixtures pin the resolution on the shape the helper will actually meet' -- i.e. an assumption, not a verified match. (2) The sibling #812 (lib/test/modules/review-stall-backstop.sh ~948-1038, scripts/background-tasks-probe-verdict.py) and #874 (lib/test/run.sh ~24212-24310, scripts/env-propagation-probe-verdict.py) fixtures never use the envelope-nested shape at all -- every one of their fixtures is the flat `{"type":"tool_use","name":...,"input":{...}}` record. They provide zero cross-validation for the envelope assumption; they simply never needed it (they only substring-match markers inside tool_use inputs, never parent_tool_use_id location). Additionally, the #858 block's own 'conformance check' (lib/test/run.sh lines 25095-25155, devflow_swv_build_ok('permitted') at line 25098) runs the census-conformance assertion ONLY against the flat 'permitted' scenario fixture -- it is never run against any of the envelope_* fixtures, so the suite provides no in-repo evidence, even structurally, that the envelope-nested fixtures were checked against the committed census. (I manually ran the same conform.py logic against a synthesized envelope_permitted fixture and it does print 'conforms', but that check is not part of the shipped suite and is a weak, key-type-only comparison that cannot detect a wrong nesting structure anyway.) So the claim's assertion of an established 'match' to production reality is not supported by either named source of truth -- the code is honest that this is an unverifiable assumption, but the claim states it as a settled fact.

results.evidence: The #858 block in lib/test/run.sh (roughly lines 25343-25410+, i.e. 'matcher-probe: both subagent-write jobs are declared...' through the 'coupled invariant' assertion) does contain multiple inline python heredocs that `import yaml` to parse .github/workflows/matcher-probe.yml: lines 25348 ('import sys, yaml'), 25375 ('import sys, yaml'), 25386 ('import sys, yaml'), and 25405 ('import re, sys, yaml'). These are unguarded (no preceding `command -v python3 && python3 -c 'import yaml'` check, unlike the guarded pattern at lib/test/run.sh:22949, 23087, 30497, 31335, 39928), so if PyYAML were absent, the heredoc would raise ImportError, python3 would exit non-zero, `$(...)` would capture empty stdout, and assert_eq would compare the expected literal (e.g. 'yes'/'coupled') against an empty string -> the assertion FAILS loudly rather than silently passing. lib/preflight.sh explicitly guarantees PyYAML on every tier (line 44: `_DEVFLOW_PREFLIGHT_GUARANTEES=(git gh jq python3 PyYAML)`; lines 190-191 print a remedy and the caller enforces exit on missing PyYAML), matching the claim's premise that PyYAML availability is a documented suite prerequisite. Minor imprecision: the specific yaml import at line 24420 (which the claim's source_file/line pointer is closest to) actually belongs to the preceding #874 block, not #858 — but the #858 block itself does independently contain four of its own `import yaml` inline helpers, so the claim's core assertion (the #858 block's python helpers import yaml to parse matcher-probe.yml, and PyYAML absence would not silently pass) holds against the actual #858-tagged assertions further down in the file.
